title: Member, not part
hook: call yourself a member of humanity, not just a part, and you'll love from the heart (Meditations 7.13)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sympatheia: everything woven together, and the weaving holy. Your line was the cup in your hand.

A spare tire is part of a car. Take it out, put in another one, and the car doesn't notice. Your hand is not like that. Cut it, and your whole body flinches; your other hand reaches over without being asked. Nobody has to remind it that it's on the same team. Marcus Aurelius noticed that in Greek, the word for a replaceable piece and the word for a living limb differ by a single letter, and he built a whole lesson out of that letter.
screen: `A SPARE TIRE.` → `A HAND THAT FLINCHES.` → `ONE LETTER APART.`

segments.voice: In Meditations seven, thirteen, Marcus says thinking beings are joined together like the limbs of one body, made to work with each other. That's an old Stoic picture of humanity: not a crowd of strangers, but one body. Then the wordplay. In Greek, a limb or member is melos; a part, a piece, is meros. Only the middle letter changes: lambda becomes rho. If you call yourself merely a part, Marcus says, you don't yet love people from the heart. Call yourself a member, a living limb, and something shifts. How do you know which you are? His test is sharp. If doing good to others doesn't yet delight you for its own sake, if you do it only because it's right, as a duty, you're still thinking like a part. A member helps the way your left hand helps your right: not as a favor, not to be thanked, because it's the same body. Marcus isn't scolding duty; doing good from duty is still good. He's pointing past it, to a place where kindness feels like taking care of yourself, because it is. Many families know this. You don't drive your sister to the airport because it's the correct thing. You drive her because she's your sister. Marcus asks what life would be like if the circle of sister were a lot wider.
screen: `ONE BODY OF THINKING BEINGS.` · `MELOS AND MEROS: ONE LETTER.` · `DOES DOING GOOD DELIGHT YOU?` · `KINDNESS AS CARE OF THE BODY.` · then, large: `A MEMBER.`

segments.voice: Feel your two hands resting, and how easily they work together, without negotiation. Bring to mind someone outside your family, a coworker, a neighbor, a stranger you saw today, and hold them the way one hand holds the other. Notice how that changes what you'd be willing to do for them.
Member. Marcus's one-letter lesson: not a replaceable part, but a living limb of one body, who loves from the heart. Today's word.
Your line: a member. One body, and the circle a little wider. That's day five hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus sometimes use the melos and meros wordplay as a reminder to help others as members of one body, the way one hand helps the other, rather than as a duty to be completed.
